sec.title: Background
sec.p: PTEN-deficient glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), therapeutic resistance, and poor prognosis. Emerging evidence suggests that dysregulation of the endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-MAVS-IFN pathway may contribute to immune evasion in cancer, but its role in PTEN-deficient GBM remains unclear.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed the immune landscape of PTEN-deficient GBM. We evaluated the effects of 5-azacytidine (5-AZA) monotherapy and its combination with EZH2 inhibition (EZH2i) on ERV reactivation, type I interferon (IFN) responses, and TME remodeling. Mechanistic studies focused on H3K27me3-mediated epigenetic regulation of ERV expression.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We found that PTEN deficiency suppresses type I IFN responses by impairing viral mimicry through dysregulation of the ERV-MAVS-IFN pathway, thereby sustaining an immunosuppressive TME. While 5-AZA alone failed to reactivate ERVs or overcome therapeutic resistance, combining it with EZH2i synergistically restored robust type I IFN signaling. This combination therapy reduced H3K27me3 levels, promoting ERV transcriptional activation and enhancing 5-AZA-induced viral mimicry. Consequently, the dual treatment reprogrammed the TME to boost antitumor immunity and suppress tumor progression.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study demonstrates that PTEN-deficient GBM evades immune surveillance by suppressing the ERV-MAVS-IFN axis. The combination of EZH2i and 5-AZA overcomes this resistance by epigenetically reactivating viral mimicry, offering a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance antitumor immunity and improve outcomes in patients with PTEN-deficient GBM.
Keywords: Tumor Microenvironment, Immunotherapy, Innate

caption.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: This study reveals that PTEN deficiency suppresses the ERV-MAVS-IFN pathway, impairing type I IFN responses and sustaining an immunosuppressive TME. While 5-AZA monotherapy fails to reactivate ERVs or overcome therapeutic resistance in PTEN-deficient GBM, combining EZH2 inhibition (EZH2i) with 5-AZA synergistically restores a robust type I IFN response. Mechanistically, EZH2i reduces H3K27me3 levels, enhancing ERV transcription and amplifying 5-AZA-induced viral mimicry, thereby reprogramming the TME to promote antitumor immunity.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: The findings uncover a novel mechanism of immune evasion in PTEN-deficient GBM and provide a rationale for targeting the ERV-MAVS-IFN pathway. The combination of EZH2i and 5-AZA may represent a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance immunotherapy responses and improve outcomes in patients with PTEN-deficient GBM. This study offers potential translational implications for other immunosuppressive cancers by leveraging epigenetic modulation to boost viral mimicry and antitumor immunity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) represents one of the most aggressive primary brain malignancies, with a universally poor prognosis and median survival of merely 12–15 months despite multimodal therapy.1,3 The tumor suppressor PTEN, among the most frequently mutated genes in primary gliomas, has emerged as a critical prognostic biomarker, with its loss consistently associated with worse clinical outcomes.4 While PTEN-deficient GBMs may initially respond to standard therapies, they invariably develop therapeutic resistance and recur.5,7 Recent advances in cancer immunotherapy have prompted investigation of various immunotherapeutic strategies targeting GBM-associated antigens, including immune checkpoint blockade, adoptive cell transfer, and oncolytic virotherapy.8,10 However, clinical trials evaluating these approaches have demonstrated limited efficacy against both PTEN-wildtype and PTEN-deficient GBMs.11,17 The profound immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) characteristic of PTEN-deficient GBM poses a particularly formidable barrier to effective immune-mediated tumor control. Overcoming this immunosuppression to elicit robust antitumor immunity therefore represents one of the most pressing challenges in neuro-oncology and cancer immunotherapy.

Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), remnants of ancient viral infections integrated into germline DNA,18 19 comprise approximately 8% of the human genome.20 These genomic elements play a crucial role in antitumor immunity by activating the RIG-I-MDA5-MAVS signaling pathway, thereby stimulating type I interferon (IFN) responses that enhance immunotherapy efficacy.21 22 The DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-azacytidine (5-AZA) has emerged as a potent inducer of ERV-mediated viral mimicry. Mechanistically, 5-AZA treatment promotes cytoplasmic accumulation of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) through ERV reactivation,23 triggering downstream interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression and robust IFN responses in GBM cells.22 24 25 These findings position 5-AZA as a promising immunotherapeutic agent capable of reprogramming the TME via IFN pathway activation. However, the therapeutic potential of 5-AZA in PTEN-deficient GBM remains uncertain. Given the established role of PTEN loss in modulating immune responses, rigorous investigation is warranted to determine whether PTEN deficiency compromises 5-AZA-induced viral mimicry and associated antitumor immunity.

The tumor suppressor PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog deleted on chromosome 10) plays a multifaceted role in regulating innate immune responses through its interaction with key IFN signaling pathways. As a critical modulator of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), PTEN facilitates nuclear translocation of this master transcription factor to drive IFN-β production and subsequent expression of ISGs.26 27 Mechanistically, PTEN deficiency disrupts this process while simultaneously impairing cGAS-STING pathway activation, collectively resulting in a profoundly suppressed IFN response.28 In GBM, PTEN deletion creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment through its detrimental effects on cGAS-STING signaling.29 This immunosuppression has direct therapeutic consequences, as evidenced by preclinical studies demonstrating that PTEN-deficient GBM tumors become resistant to STING agonist-mediated enhancement of temozolomide efficacy.30 Emerging evidence has highlighted the critical role of nuclear PTEN in epigenetic regulation and genome maintenance. Beyond its canonical cytoplasmic functions, nuclear PTEN actively participates in histone modification and chromatin remodeling, thereby influencing transcriptional programs. Importantly, PTEN localizes to the nucleus where it physically associates with the spliceosome machinery and cyclin B1-CDK1 complex to regulate RNA processing and cell cycle progression. Furthermore, nuclear PTEN contributes to genomic stability by facilitating DNA repair mechanisms and enhancing cellular sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents.31,34 These findings establish nuclear PTEN as a multifaceted regulator operating at the interface of epigenetic control and genome integrity.

Our study establishes a novel mechanism by which PTEN regulates type I IFN responses and shapes the TME through modulation of the dsRNA-MAVS-IFN pathway. Most significantly, we present the first evidence that combined EZH2 inhibition (EZH2i) with 5-AZA treatment synergistically activates viral mimicry pathways, resulting in a potent type I IFN response. This combinatorial approach effectively reprograms the immunosuppressive TME, enhancing antitumor immunity and suppressing progression in PTEN-deficient GBM. These findings identify a promising therapeutic strategy that overcomes the limitations of single-agent approaches in this treatment-resistant malignancy.

sec.title: Data acquisition and processing
sec.p: Transcriptomic data from patients with GBM were obtained from three major publicly available genomic repositories: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/), the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA; http://www.cgga.org.cn), and the Gene Expression Omnibus (accession GSE16011; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). These datasets collectively provided comprehensive RNA sequencing profiles of GBM specimens. To ensure analytical rigor, we performed systematic data preprocessing and integration using the R package “tinyarray”, which included quality control, normalization, and batch effect correction to generate a robust dataset for subsequent analyses.

sec.title: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis
sec.p: We performed Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) to systematically evaluate whether predefined gene sets showed statistically significant, concordant differences between PTEN high-expression and low-expression groups. The analysis was conducted using the “h.all.v2023.2.Hs.symbols.gmt” gene set collection from the Molecular Signatures Database, which contains well-curated hallmark gene sets representing specific biological states and processes. Gene sets with a false discovery rate q value<0.05 were considered statistically significant, following established computational biology standards for pathway analysis.

sec.title: Reagents and materials
sec.p: A comprehensive list of all chemical compounds and antibodies employed in this study, including their sources and catalog numbers, is provided in online supplemental table 1. This includes detailed specifications for the 5-AZA and EZH2i compounds used in our therapeutic experiments, as well as complete antibody information for all immunological and molecular biology applications.

sec.title: Cell lines and cell culture
sec.p: The human U251 and murine GL261 GBM cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, Virginia, USA). Cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Hyclone), penicillin (100 U/mL), and streptomycin (100 µg/mL) (Sigma-Aldrich) under standard culture conditions (37°C, 5% CO2 in a humidified atmosphere). All cell lines underwent regular Mycoplasma testing using PCR-based detection methods to ensure contamination-free cultures prior to experimental use.

sec.title: Knockdown and overexpression experiments
sec.p: For PTEN knockdown experiments, we designed specific shRNA constructs targeting murine PTEN along with non-targeting control shRNAs (GeneCopoeia, Guangzhou, China). Lentiviral particles were produced by co-transfecting 293T cells with shRNA plasmids and the packaging plasmids VSVG, PLP1, and PLP2 using Lipofectamine 3000 transfection reagent. Viral supernatants were harvested 72 hours post-transfection, filtered through 0.45 µm membranes, and used to transduce GL261 cells. Stable cell lines were established through puromycin selection (2 µg/mL) for 14 days. For PTEN overexpression, U251 cells were transduced with lentiviral vectors containing full-length human PTEN (Miao Ling Biotechnology, Wuhan, China). The efficiency of both knockdown and overexpression was quantitatively validated by quantitative reverse-transcription real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of PTEN messenger RNA (mRNA) levels, with all experiments including appropriate negative controls.

sec.title: Gene silencing with small interfering RNA
sec.p: To investigate the functional roles of key signaling molecules, we performed small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated knockdown of MYD88, MAVS, and STING in U251-PTEN cells. Commercially synthesized siRNA duplexes (Ribobio, Guangzhou, China), along with a non-targeting control siRNA, were transfected into cells using Lipofectamine 3000 reagent according to the manufacturer’s optimized protocol. Knockdown efficiency was rigorously validated at the protein level by quantitative Western blot analysis, ensuring effective silencing of each target gene before functional assays.

sec.title: Quantitative reverse-transcription real-time PCR
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated from cultured cells using TRIzol reagent (Life Technologies) following the manufacturer’s protocol. For gene expression analysis, complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 µg total RNA using reverse transcriptase, followed by quantitative reverse-transcription real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) using SYBR Green chemistry on a QuantStudio system (Applied Biosystems). Primer pairs were designed using Primer Express V.2.0 software (Applied Biosystems) with stringent criteria for specificity and efficiency. All gene expression levels were normalized to the geometric mean of GAPDH reference transcripts, with relative quantification performed using the comparative Ct (2(−ΔΔCt)) method. Complete primer sequences are provided in online supplemental table 2.

For mitochondrial RNA analysis, cytosolic RNA fractions were isolated from U251 cells using differential centrifugation. Strand-specific cDNA synthesis was performed using SuperScript IV reverse transcriptase with primers containing CMV promoter sequences (online supplemental table 3). Subsequent qRT-PCR amplification employed strand-specific primer sets (online supplemental table 4) as previously validated.35 Each experiment included no-template controls and melt curve analysis to ensure amplification specificity.

sec.title: ELISA
sec.p: For IFN-β detection, conditioned media were collected and clarified by centrifugation (10,000×g, 10 min, 4°C) to remove particulate matter. IFN-β concentrations were then determined using a commercially available quantitative ELISA kit (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA) according to the manufacturer’s specifications. All samples were analyzed in technical duplicates, with absorbance measurements performed at 450 nm using a microplate reader. A standard curve generated from recombinant IFN-β was included in each assay to ensure accurate quantification, with sensitivity thresholds as specified by the manufacturer.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: Protein extracts were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE, 8–12% gradient gels) under reducing conditions and electrotransferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat dry milk in TBST (tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer overnight at 4°C. After three 10 min washes with TBST, membranes were probed with species-matched horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5,000 dilution) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate (Pierce) and imaged with a ChemiDoc imaging system (Bio-Rad). Band intensities were quantified using ImageLab software (Bio-Rad), with normalization to loading controls.

sec.title: Mouse and xenograft tumor models
sec.p: All animal experiments were conducted in strict accordance with protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital. 6–8 weeks old male C57BL/6 mice (Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center) were used for both subcutaneous and orthotopic tumor models. For subcutaneous implantation, 1×106 GL261 cells (either shNC or shPTEN) in 100 µL phosphate buffered saline (PBS) were injected into the right flank, followed by intraperitoneal administration of 10 mg/kg anti-IFNAR1 antibody or PBS control three times weekly. Intracranial tumors were established by stereotactic injection of 1×105 tumor cells in 5 µL PBS into the right striatum (coordinates: 2.0 mm lateral, 0.5 mm anterior to bregma, 3.0 mm depth), with tumor progression monitored by serial bioluminescence imaging. Therapeutic interventions included: 5-AZA monotherapy (3 mg/kgintraperitoneal (i.p.), days 5–8 and 10–13; n=7) and combination therapy with 5-AZA (3 mg/kg) plus EZH2i (100 mg/kg) on days 4-7 and 10–13 (n=7). Terminal tissues were collected at defined endpoints (20% weight loss or neurological symptoms) for histological processing.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: Tumor specimens from treatment cohorts (GL261-shNC/shPTEN models receiving anti-IFNAR1 antibody, PBS, EZH2i, 5-AZA, or combination therapy) were processed into single-cell suspensions through mechanical dissociation followed by enzymatic digestion (2 mg/mL collagenase IV, 0.02 mg/mL DNase I in DMEM/5% FBS) at 37°C for 45 minutes. After erythrocyte lysis, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies (diluted in PBS/2% FBS) for surface markers for 30 minutes on ice. For intracellular staining (including dsRNA detection using J2 antibody), cells were fixed in 75% ethanol (−20°C, 60 minutes) and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (RT, 15 minutes). All samples were acquired on a CytoFLEX SRT flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) with compensation controls, and data were analyzed using CytExpert software (V.2.4) with appropriate gating strategies to exclude doublets and dead cells.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: For subcellular localization studies, cells were plated at a density of 2×105 cells per glass-bottom dish (MatTek Corporation) and allowed to adhere for 24 hours. Following fixation with 4% paraformaldehyde (15 minutes, room temperature), cells were permeabilized and blocked with 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% bovine serum albumin in PBS (30 minutes, 37°C). Primary antibody incubation was performed using anti-dsRNA J2 antibody (1:1,000 dilution, 1 hour, 37°C), followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:1,000, 1 hour, room temperature) in PBS/1% BSA. Nuclei were counterstained with 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI, 1:1,000, 5 minutes), with thorough PBS washes between each step. High-resolution images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 780 confocal microscope equipped with 405 nm and 488 nm lasers, using a 63×oil-immersion objective (NA 1.4). Z-stack images were collected at 0.5 µm intervals and processed using ZEN software (Zeiss) for maximum intensity projections.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software (V.10.0). Parametric data following normal distribution (assessed by Shapiro-Wilk test) were analyzed using either unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test for pairwise comparisons or one-way analysis of variance with Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple group comparisons. Non-parametric data were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U test (for tumor growth curves) or Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction, as appropriate. Survival analyses were performed using the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test with Kaplan-Meier curves. Data are presented as mean±SEM unless otherwise specified, with significance levels denoted as *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, and ****p<0.0001.

sec.title: PTEN deficiency suppresses intrinsic IFN signaling in GBM
sec.p: To investigate PTEN’s role in GBM immune regulation, we performed GSEA using the hallmark gene set collection (“h.all.v2023.2.Hs.symbols.gmt”) across multiple datasets (CGGA, GSE16011, and TCGA-GBM). Stratification by PTEN expression (high vs low) and mutation status (sense vs nonsense) revealed significant enrichment of “INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE” and “INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE” gene signatures in PTEN-high samples (figure 1A). Notably, PTEN-intact tumors in the TCGA-GBM dataset showed specific enrichment for IFN response pathways (figure 1B), suggesting PTEN’s potential role in modulating IFN signaling.

sec.p: Clinical correlation analysis using an 80-sample tissue microarray (77 gliomas, 3 normal controls) demonstrated a significant positive association between PTEN and IFN-β protein expression (Pearson’s R=0.3718, p<0.001) (figure 1C and D). This clinical observation prompted us to experimentally validate PTEN’s functional role in IFN regulation using isogenic GBM models.

In mechanistic studies, PTEN knockdown in GL261 (PTEN-wildtype) cells significantly reduced IFNB1 mRNA expression (qRT-PCR) and IFN-β secretion (ELISA) (figure 1E). Conversely, PTEN overexpression in U251 (PTEN-null) cells robustly enhanced both IFNB1 transcript levels and IFN-β protein production (figure 1F). These complementary gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments establish PTEN as a positive regulator of intrinsic type I IFN signaling in GBM cells.

sec.title: PTEN deficiency impairs dsRNA-MAVS pathway-mediated type I IFN responses
sec.p: Type I IFNs exert their biological effects through JAK-STAT signaling, inducing an ISG program critical for antiviral defense.36 We investigated whether PTEN regulates this pathway in GBM. PTEN overexpression in U251 cells significantly upregulated ISGs (IFIT1, ISG15, and CXCL10), an effect abrogated by JAK inhibition (ruxolitinib, 5 uM) or TBK1 inhibition (MRT67307, 1 µM) (figure 2A), indicating PTEN maintains ISG expression through both JAK1 and TBK1. Western blot analysis revealed reduced phosphorylation of TBK1 and IRF3 in GL261-shPTEN cells, while U251-PTEN cells showed enhanced activation of these pathway components (figure 2B), demonstrating PTEN’s role in regulating the TBK1-IRF3 axis.

sec.p: Mechanistic studies using siRNA knockdown revealed MAVS, but not MYD88 or STING, as essential for PTEN-mediated induction of IFNB1 and CXCL10 (figure 2C), implicating the dsRNA-sensing pathway. Since ERVs form immunostimulatory dsRNA recognized by RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS,24 37 we examined dsRNA accumulation using J2 antibody staining. RNase III (dsRNA-specific) but not RNase H (DNA-RNA hybrid-specific) treatment significantly reduced dsRNA foci in both U251-PTEN and GL261-shNC cells (figure 2D and E). Correspondingly, PTEN could positively regulate ERV transcription in both U251 and GL261 cells (figure 2F and G), establishing ERV-derived dsRNA as the primary activator of MAVS-dependent IFN signaling in PTEN-proficient GBM.

Although mitochondrial bidirectional transcription generates dsRNA,38 39 pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial RNA polymerase40 specifically reduced mitochondrial transcripts without affecting ERV expression (online supplemental figure 1A, B), dsRNA levels (online supplemental figure 1C), or ISG induction (online supplemental figure 1D). Strand-specific quantitative PCR confirmed no PTEN-dependent changes in mitochondrial RNA (ND-1, ND-4, ND-6) (online supplemental figure 1E). These results definitively identify ERVs, not mitochondrial RNA, as the major source of immunostimulatory dsRNA driving PTEN-dependent IFN activation in GBM.

sec.title: PTEN deficiency promotes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by attenuating IFN responses
sec.p: To determine whether PTEN regulates GBM progression through IFN-dependent mechanisms, we established syngeneic tumors in C57BL/6 mice using GL261 cells with either intact (shNC) or depleted PTEN (shPTEN). Mice were treated with anti-IFNAR1 blocking antibody (10 mg/kg, 3×weekly) or PBS control. PTEN-deficient tumors exhibited significantly increased growth compared with controls, as measured by both tumor volume and weight (p<0.01). Importantly, IFNAR1 blockade abolished this difference, with comparable tumor growth observed between shNC+anti-IFNAR1 and shPTEN+anti-IFNAR1 groups. Furthermore, anti-IFNAR1 treatment accelerated tumor progression in both shNC and shPTEN models relative to PBS controls (figure 3A and B). These findings were validated in IFNAR1-KO mice, where PTEN status no longer influenced tumor growth kinetics (figure 3C and D), demonstrating that PTEN-mediated tumor suppression requires functional type I IFN signaling.

sec.p: Immunophenotyping of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes revealed that PTEN deficiency skewed the immune landscape toward immunosuppression. Specifically, shPTEN tumors showed elevated frequencies of CD4+T cells and regulatory T cells (Tregs), along with reduced CD8+T cell infiltration and cytotoxic granzyme B+CD8+T cells (p<0.05). Consequently, the CD8/Treg ratio, a critical metric of antitumor immunity, was markedly diminished in PTEN-deficient tumors (p<0.01). Strikingly, IFNAR1 neutralization equalized these differences, indicating that PTEN sustains immunogenic TME properties in an IFN-dependent manner (figure 3E-J,online supplemental figure 2).

To extend these findings to human GBM, we analyzed immune infiltration patterns across three independent cohorts (CGGA, GSE16011, and TCGA). Single-sample GSEA demonstrated that PTEN-high tumors were enriched for central memory CD8+T cells, effector memory CD8+T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells (p<0.05), cell types associated with improved antitumor immunity (figure 3K). Collectively, these results establish PTEN as a key regulator of IFN-mediated immune surveillance in GBM, whose loss fosters an immunosuppressive TME conducive to tumor progression.

sec.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals PTEN deficiency shapes an immunosuppressive GBM microenvironment through impaired type I IFN signaling
sec.p: To characterize the TME in PTEN-deficient GBM, we established four experimental groups using the GL261 murine glioma model (1): wild-type (WT) mice bearing control tumors (WT_shNC), (2) WT mice bearing PTEN-knockdown tumors (WT_shP), (3) IFNAR1-knockout mice bearing control tumors (KO_shNC), and (4) IFNAR1-knockout mice bearing PTEN-knockdown tumors (KO_shP). CD45+immune cells were isolated from tumor tissues by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and subjected to single-cell RNA sequencing.

Comparative analysis revealed significant alterations in immune cell composition and function associated with PTEN status. The shPTEN group exhibited reduced T-cell infiltration and attenuated inflammatory responses across T cells, NK cells, and myeloid populations compared with controls (figure 4A–C, online supplemental figure 3A–C). In the myeloid compartment, PTEN deficiency led to a marked decrease in IFN-responsive macrophages (Macro_Ifitm3+), with corresponding reductions in inflammatory and IFN-γ responses (figure 4D–G, online supplemental figure 3D–F). Notably, these effects were abrogated in IFNAR1-knockout mice (KO_shNC and KO_shP groups), demonstrating the essential role of type I IFN signaling. While the proportion of antitumor Macro_Cxcl9+macrophages was numerically increased in PTEN-deficient tumors, these cells showed impaired functional activity (figure 4E, online supplemental figure 3B), suggesting that PTEN maintains macrophage effector functions through IFN-dependent mechanisms.

sec.p: Analysis of lymphoid populations revealed that PTEN deficiency significantly compromised CD8+T cell responses, with reduced frequencies of cytotoxic subsets (Ccl3+, Ccl5+, Gzma+) and IFN-responsive populations (Ifitm1+). Similarly, antitumor NK cell subsets (Gzma+, Gzmc+, Xcl1+) were diminished in PTEN-deficient tumors (figure 4H–N, online supplemental figure 4). Intriguingly, while IFNAR1 knockout resulted in decreased CD8+T cell infiltration overall, the remaining cells predominantly lacked markers of effector function (figure 4J and N), indicating that intact IFN signaling is required for both recruitment and activation of cytotoxic T cells.

These findings collectively demonstrate that PTEN deficiency promotes an immunosuppressive TME in GBM through mechanisms dependent on type I IFN signaling. The impaired immune responses observed in both myeloid and lymphoid compartments suggest that PTEN plays a crucial role in maintaining antitumor immunity by sustaining IFN-mediated activation of tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Our results provide novel insights into the immunological consequences of PTEN loss in GBM and highlight the importance of the PTEN-IFN axis in shaping the TME.

sec.title: PTEN deficiency restricts 5-AZA-induced ERV expression through DNMT1-mediated DNA methylation
sec.p: DNA methylation represents a critical epigenetic mechanism regulating ERV expression.2441,43 As 5-AZA, a DNMT1 inhibitor, is known to activate ERVs and subsequent immune responses,22 24 43 we investigated whether PTEN regulates ERV expression through DNMT1-mediated DNA methylation. Using flow cytometry with the dsRNA-specific J2 antibody, we observed that 5-AZA treatment significantly increased J2 mean fluorescence intensity in control GL261-shNC cells (figure 5A). In striking contrast, PTEN-deficient GL261-shPTEN cells showed no response to 5-AZA treatment. This pattern was confirmed in U251 cells, where PTEN knockout abolished 5-AZA-induced dsRNA production, while PTEN overexpression restored this response (figure 5B). These results demonstrate that PTEN is essential for 5-AZA-mediated dsRNA induction.

sec.p: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis revealed that basal ERV expression levels were significantly lower in PTEN-deficient GL261-shPTEN cells compared with controls (figure 5C). Conversely, PTEN-overexpressing U251 cells showed elevated ERV expression. Following 5-AZA treatment, PTEN-deficient cells failed to upregulate ERVs to the same extent as controls, while PTEN-overexpressing cells exhibited enhanced ERV induction (figure 5C). These findings collectively demonstrate that PTEN maintains cellular responsiveness to 5-AZA-mediated ERV activation. Our results establish a novel role for PTEN in regulating ERV expression through DNMT1-independent mechanisms. The impaired response to 5-AZA in PTEN-deficient cells suggests that PTEN status may significantly influence the efficacy of epigenetic therapies in cancer treatment.

sec.title: EZH2 inhibition restores 5-AZA-induced ERV expression by reducing H3K27me3 in PTEN-deficient GBM
sec.p: Emerging evidence indicates that nuclear PTEN plays a crucial role in maintaining chromosomal stability.33 Given that histone H3 trimethylation represents another key epigenetic mechanism regulating ERV expression,44 45 we hypothesized that nuclear PTEN might influence ERV expression through histone modifications. Western blot analysis revealed that PTEN overexpression specifically reduced H3K27me3 levels, with minimal effects on other H3 methylation sites (figure 5D and E).

Since EZH2 serves as the primary methyltransferase for H3K27me3-mediated transcriptional silencing, we investigated whether PTEN regulates EZH2 expression and activity. Notably, phosphorylation of EZH2 at Thr367 (p-EZH2), which enhances nuclear localization and enzymatic activity,46,48 was significantly increased in PTEN-deficient GL261-shPTEN cells and decreased in PTEN-overexpressing U251 cells compared with their respective controls (figure 5F). These findings suggest PTEN may function as a protein phosphatase to dephosphorylate EZH2 at Thr367, thereby alleviating ERV transcriptional silencing.

To test this hypothesis, we treated U251 and GL261-shPTEN cells with the EZH2 inhibitor EPZ-6438 (EZH2i, 10 µM) in combination with 5-AZA (1 µM). Quantitative RT-PCR demonstrated that dual treatment synergistically enhanced expression of both ISGs (figure 5G) and ERVs (figure 5H and I) compared with single-agent treatments or controls. Immunofluorescence staining with the dsRNA-specific J2 antibody confirmed these findings, showing significantly increased fluorescence intensity following combination therapy (figure 5J). These results demonstrate that EZH2 inhibition can overcome PTEN deficiency by reducing H3K27me3 levels, thereby restoring 5-AZA-induced ERV expression in GBM. Our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which PTEN regulates the epigenetic landscape through EZH2 phosphorylation and suggest combination epigenetic therapy as a potential strategy for PTEN-deficient GBMs.

sec.title: Synergistic effects of EZH2 inhibition and 5-AZA in reversing immunosuppression and inhibiting PTEN-deficient GBM growth
sec.p: Our study demonstrates that combined EZH2i and 5-AZA treatment effectively overcomes PTEN deficiency-mediated resistance in GBM through TME remodeling. Using an orthotopic GBM model, we first evaluated 5-AZA monotherapy (3 mg/kg/day, i.p.) in mice bearing either control (GL261-shNC) or PTEN-knockdown (GL261-shPTEN) tumors (n=7/group). While 5-AZA significantly prolonged survival in control tumors, it showed no therapeutic benefit in PTEN-deficient tumors (median survival: shNC+control, 27 days; shNC+5 AZA, 35 days; shPTEN+control, 24 days; shPTEN+5 AZA, 27 days; figure 6A and B). Longitudinal bioluminescence imaging revealed comparable tumor progression at baseline (day 5), but by day 14, 5-AZA selectively inhibited control tumor growth while showing no efficacy against PTEN-deficient tumors (figure 6C), as confirmed by histopathological analysis (figure 6D).

sec.p: To overcome this resistance, we combined 5-AZA with EZH2i (100 mg/kg/day, i.p.) in PTEN-deficient tumors (n=7/group). The combination therapy demonstrated remarkable synergy, significantly extending survival compared with either monotherapy (median survival: control group, 19 days; DNMT1 group, 20 days; EHZ2i group, 22 days; combinational group, 30 days; figure 6E) and inducing marked tumor regression (figure 6F). Flow cytometry analysis revealed profound TME remodeling, with the combination therapy increasing cytotoxic CD8+T cell infiltration, granzyme B+CD8+ T cells, and IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells, while reducing immunosuppressive populations (CD4+T cells and Tregs cells; figure 6G and H). The CD8+/Treg ratio improved, indicating a fundamental shift toward an immunostimulatory microenvironment.

Antibody depletion studies confirmed that CD8+T cells are the primary effectors of therapeutic efficacy, as depletion of CD8+T cells abrogated the survival benefit of 5-AZA with EZH2i combination treatment, while depletion of CD4+T cells or NK cells showed no significant effect (median survival: isotype control 30 days; anti-CD8 group, 20 days; anti-CD4 group, 29 days; anti-NK group, 27 days; figure 6I). These findings establish that combined epigenetic therapy overcomes PTEN deficiency by selectively enhancing CD8+T cell-mediated antitumor immunity, providing a promising therapeutic strategy for this treatment-resistant GBM subtype.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: GBM, the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor, frequently exhibits PTEN functional loss in both primary and recurrent cases.49 Our study addresses the critical need for effective therapeutic strategies against PTEN-deficient GBM through three key discoveries: first, we demonstrate for the first time that PTEN deficiency suppresses type I IFN responses and promotes an immunosuppressive TME in GBM. Second, we establish that nuclear PTEN expression is essential for 5-AZA-mediated induction of ERV expression, providing a mechanistic explanation for the therapeutic resistance observed in PTEN-deficient GBM. Most importantly, we show that EZH2i reduces p-EZH2, thereby functionally compensating for nuclear PTEN loss and restoring 5-AZA-induced ERV expression in PTEN-deficient tumors. The clinical significance of our findings lies in the synergistic antitumor effects achieved through combined EZH2i and 5-AZA therapy. This combination treatment significantly enhances antitumor immune responses and improves therapeutic outcomes in PTEN-deficient GBM models, offering a promising precision medicine approach for this treatment-resistant GBM subtype.

A previous study has reported that pharmacologic activation of p53 induced the expression of ERVs via increased occupancy on ERV promoters and inhibition of two major ERV repressors, histone demethylase LSD1 and DNA methyltransferase DNMT1.50 The molecular landscape of GBM is further characterized by frequent TERT promoter mutations, which represent the most common genetic alteration in both medulloblastoma and glioma, occurring in approximately 80% of primary GBM cases.51 These TERT abnormalities, along with p53 mutations, constitute fundamental drivers of gliomagenesis.52 Notably, wild-type p53 exerts tumor-suppressive control over TERT expression through a dual mechanism: SP1-dependent transcriptional repression and regulation via E3 ubiquitin protein ligase-mediated degradation pathways.53

Extensive clinical evidence has established that robust T-cell infiltration positively correlates with improved responses to immunotherapy across multiple cancer types.54 Previous investigations have demonstrated that genomic deletions or reduced expression of PTEN are associated with impaired T-cell trafficking and the development of an immunosuppressive TME in various malignancies.55,58 Mechanistically, PTEN has been shown to critically regulate the activity and function of multiple T-cell subsets, including CD4+T cells, CD8+T cells, and Tregs.56 59 Our current findings significantly extend these observations by demonstrating that PTEN maintains T-cell infiltration in GBM through the ERV-IFN pathway. This discovery aligns with the well-established role of type I IFN signaling in mediating T-cell recruitment and activation within the TME.54 Importantly, our results provide compelling evidence that PTEN-deficient GBM develops its characteristic immunosuppressive TME in a manner dependent on type I IFN responses, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanistic link between PTEN status and immune evasion in GBM.

5-AZA, a pyrimidine nucleoside analog,60 mediates its antitumor effects through global DNA hypomethylation and epigenetic reprogramming in cancer cells.61 This demethylating agent has been shown to activate ERV expression via viral mimicry, thereby stimulating type I IFN responses and antitumor immunity.22 24 While clinically approved for myelodysplastic syndromes and demonstrating efficacy in delaying progression to acute myeloid leukemia,62 63 the therapeutic potential of 5-AZA in solid tumors, particularly GBM, remains largely unexplored.64 65 Emerging preclinical evidence suggests that 5-AZA may synergize with immune checkpoint blockade and other immunotherapies by enhancing tumor immunogenicity.22 24 66 Our findings reveal a critical limitation of 5-AZA monotherapy in PTEN-deficient GBM, where elevated H3K27me3 levels impair ERV induction despite effective DNA demethylation. These results establish PTEN as a key determinant of 5-AZA responsiveness in GBM and suggest that combination strategies targeting both DNA methylation and H3K27me3 may be required to overcome resistance in PTEN-deficient tumors. The mechanistic link between PTEN status and epigenetic therapy response identified in this study has important implications for the clinical development of 5-AZA-based regimens in GBM and other PTEN-deficient malignancies.

EZH2, a critical epigenetic modulator, regulates gene expression through its catalytic activity mediating H3K27me3 deposition and subsequent transcriptional silencing.67,69 Our study reveals that nuclear PTEN negatively regulates EZH2 activity by reducing phosphorylation at Thr367 (p-EZH2), thereby decreasing global H3K27me3 levels. This finding is particularly significant given the well-established association between elevated EZH2 expression/H3K27me3 marks and poor clinical outcomes in gliomas and other malignancies,70,72 which has positioned EZH2 as an attractive therapeutic target.73 74 Emerging evidence suggests EZH2i exerts antitumor effects partly through viral mimicry—the derepression of ERVs and subsequent activation of IFN signaling.75 76 Our work demonstrates that combined EZH2i and 5-AZA treatment effectively restores ERV expression and triggers type I IFN responses in PTEN-deficient GBM, overcoming the epigenetic blockade imposed by PTEN loss. These preclinical findings align with ongoing clinical trials evaluating EZH2i across various cancers77,79 and are particularly relevant for glioma treatment, as our data show this combination strategy successfully reverses immunosuppression in PTEN-deficient GBM by remodeling the TME and inhibiting tumor progression.80 Compared with DNMT inhibitor (5-AZA) monotherapy, the combination of 5-AZA and EZH2 inhibition induced synergistic gene expression activation, which correlated with enhanced chromatin accessibility at functionally relevant genomic loci. Mechanistically, EZH2 blockade alleviates the repressive H3K27me3 mark at bivalent chromatin domains, thereby overcoming the limited transcriptional reactivation observed with DNMTi treatment alone.81 This synergistic effect of combination strategy can reduce the therapeutic dose of each agent, which helps to reduce the potential systemic toxicities of 5-AZA. The mechanistic insights provided by our study strongly support the clinical investigation of EZH2i/5-AZA combination therapy for patients with PTEN-deficient GBM, offering a rational, biomarker-driven approach to overcome resistance to epigenetic therapies in this aggressive brain tumor subtype.

While a previous study demonstrated that combined EZH2 inhibition and 5-AZA treatment enhanced viral mimicry through NFAT:AP-1 signaling in colorectal cancer,42 our current work significantly expands on these findings in several critical aspects. First, we establish a novel therapeutic application for PTEN-deficient GBM, whereas prior research focused exclusively on colorectal cancer. Second, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of TME immunomodulation and therapeutic efficacy, going beyond the epigenetic mechanisms emphasized in previous work. Third, we elucidate the specific role of PTEN in regulating p-EZH2 and H3K27me3 dynamics, mechanisms not previously explored in the context of 5-AZA-induced ERV expression. Most importantly, our research demonstrates the clinical translational potential of targeting the ERV-MAVS-IFN pathway in PTEN-deficient GBM, representing both a mechanistic advancement and therapeutic application of earlier foundational discoveries. These findings collectively provide a more complete understanding of how combined epigenetic therapy can overcome tumor-intrinsic immunosuppression while offering clinically actionable strategies for GBM treatment.

Several important limitations of our study should be acknowledged. First, although we identified nuclear PTEN as a key regulator of the p-EZH2-H3K27me3-ERVs axis, direct mechanistic evidence through rescue experiments—such as PTEN reconstitution or nuclear-specific PTEN modulation—was not performed. Second, while ERVs are known to activate type I IFN responses via the cGAS-STING pathway, the specific contribution of this signaling cascade to the observed immune activation in our model remains to be elucidated. Third, our therapeutic intervention was initiated during early tumor proliferation (day 4 post-implantation), and the efficacy of this regimen in fully established tumors (days 7–8) warrants further investigation. Fourth, the potential synergistic effects of combining EZH2i and 5-AZA with immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, anti-programmed cell death protein-1) remain unexplored and represent a promising avenue for future research. Additionally, since ERVs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the human genome and contain highly repetitive sequences,82 developing effective methods to knock out or knock down a group of ERVs presents substantial technical challenges. Consequently, we are unable to adequately control the off-target effects induced by 5-AZA treatment. Finally, while direct evidence linking PTEN deficiency to alterations in H3K9 methylation or acetylation remains unreported, we hypothesize that PTEN may either interact with histone-modifying enzymes or indirectly modulate upstream components of related signaling pathways. Despite these limitations, our conclusions regarding the efficacy of combined epigenetic therapy in PTEN-deficient GBM remain robust. These findings not only highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the EZH2-ERV-IFN axis but also underscore the need for further mechanistic studies to optimize this treatment strategy for clinical translation. Future work should focus on addressing these gaps to enhance our understanding of PTEN-deficient GBM biology and refine combination therapy approaches.

Our study establishes nuclear PTEN as a critical determinant of 5-AZA-induced ERV expression in GBM, demonstrating that combined EZH2i and 5-AZA treatment effectively overcomes PTEN deficiency by restoring ERV-mediated viral mimicry and subsequent type I IFN responses. This epigenetic combination therapy significantly enhances antitumor immunity through TME remodeling and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in PTEN-deficient GBM models. These findings position the EZH2i/5-AZA combination as a promising biomarker-driven strategy for PTEN-deficient GBM, addressing a critical unmet need in this treatment-resistant patient population. The mechanistic insights and preclinical evidence presented here provide a strong rationale for clinical translation of this epigenetic immunotherapy approach.
